newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Vietnam currency drops sharply against U.S. dollar.
newsitem.headline: Vietnam currency drops sharply against U.S. dollar.

text.p: Vietnam's currency, the dong, dropped sharply on Wednesday against the dollar, reaching a level close to bottom of a new interbank trading band announced earlier this week, dealers said.
The dong was changing hands at around 11,600-11,635 per dollar in thin trade, against an official daily pivot rate of 11,096. It has fallen around 4.8 percent over the past two days.
"There's a kind of panic in the market. Everyone needs dollars," said Shanker Mahadevan at Credit Lyonnais.
"It's all been one way today," said David Pollitt, Treasury Manager at Hongkong Bank in Ho Chi Minh City. "People want to find a level, but the level is in free fall at the moment."
Traders said there had been very little two-way business on Wednesday. One estimated that total volume was unlikely to have exceeded $1 million.
Treasury analysts said they expected the central bank to intervene, selling dollars to relieve downward pressure on the dong, possibly as early as tomorrow.
The bank was not seen intervening on Wednesday.

Analysts said the central bank could also lower the dong's official floor, which was set at 11,650 per dollar after the interbank trading band was widened to five percent either side of the daily indicative rate from one percent.
The State Bank of Vietnam has been seeking a gradual depreciation of the currency and has denied repeatedly that a devaluation is on the cards.

The move was seen as a measure to help the currency keep pace with much lower black market rates. Wednesday's sharp slide on the interbank market took the dong below black market levels of around 11,450 per dollar.
The dong's stability at about 11,000 to the dollar since 1994, combined with high inflation, led to a real appreciation of about 10 percent against currencies of Vietnam's main trading partners.
Analysts say the government is hoping that a gradual depreciation will make exports cheaper, thereby helping chip away at a trade deficit which reached $4 billion in 1996.
